# Rosie's Cancer Came Back After Her AI-Designed Vaccine, and Her Owner Just Raised $4 Million

Published Aug 18, 2026 11:10 PM EDT By Amelia Palmer

Image: ABLO PORCIUNCULA | AFP via Getty Images

ABLO PORCIUNCULA | AFP via Getty Images

In March, a Sydney tech entrepreneur with no biology training became a global story. Paul Conyngham had used AI tools to help design a personalized mRNA cancer vaccine for his rescue dog Rosie, who had aggressive mast cell cancer and a prognosis measured in months. Several of her tumors shrank. OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman called it an amazing story to his millions of followers.

Five months later, the company built on her case launched with a $4 million seed round led by Founders Fund. The announcement carries a detail that most of the viral coverage never reached: Rosie's cancer came back.

## What Actually Happened in Rosie's Treatment

The version that circulated online was compressed a great deal.

Rosie was an eight-year-old Staffordshire bull terrier cross diagnosed with mast cell cancer, the most common canine skin cancer. Surgery and chemotherapy slowed the disease without stopping it.

Conyngham, who has 17 years of machine learning experience, paid about $3,000 to have Rosie's tumor DNA and healthy DNA sequenced at the University of New South Wales. He used AI to sift through thousands of mutations for neoantigens—mutated proteins that appear only on cancer cells—and used protein-structure prediction to guess which would be visible to her immune system.

He did not make a vaccine himself. Researchers at UNSW reviewed the data and built the mRNA construct in a university lab, with Pall Thordarson, director of the UNSW RNA Institute, leading that work. According to Reason, Conyngham used ChatGPT and AlphaFold to identify mutated tumor proteins and then Grok to design the final construct, and obtaining Australian ethics approval took him three months and a 100-page document.

Rosie received her first injection in December 2025 at a veterinary facility in Queensland, with a booster the following month. The Y Combinator listing for the resulting company describes it as what is believed to be the first fully computationally designed mRNA cancer vaccine administered to a dog, and notes that several tumors shrank significantly.

Conyngham has consistently declined to call it a cure.

## Remission, Then Relapse

The company's launch announcement states it directly: Rosie entered remission, but her cancer returned following a later surgery. The release is titled around her legacy and writes about her in the past tense, saying her story may have ended while the work it produced continues. The company has not publicly stated what ultimately happened to her or when.

That ambiguity matters less than what the case can and cannot show. There was no control group, no comparison animal, and no way to separate the vaccine's effect from surgery, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, or the natural variability of an individual tumor.

Key clinical details, including the grade of Rosie's tumor, have not been made public. Grade is one of the strongest predictors of outcome in canine mast cell disease, and without it, the response is difficult to interpret.

As recently as June, Australian broadcaster ABC reported on the case as a success story while scientists involved argued that regulatory hurdles were slowing similar work in humans.

## From One Dog to a Venture-Backed Platform

Gamgee, founded by Conyngham, joined Y Combinator's Summer 2026 batch and launched publicly on Aug. 17. Alongside Founders Fund, the round drew investment from Celine Halioua of canine longevity company Loyal, Steve Eidelman of Modern Animal, Dropbox co-founder Arash Ferdowsi, and Gokul Rajaram.

The model industrializes what Conyngham did by hand. The company sequences each dog's tumor and matched healthy tissue, identifies tumor-specific neoantigens, and designs a personalized mRNA vaccine intended to train the immune system to attack those targets.

Clinical studies are running in Australia in collaboration with UNSW, the University of Queensland, and the Garvan Institute of Medical Research. Enrollment is currently limited to eastern Australia; participating dogs receive the investigational vaccine at no cost, and eligibility is determined by the study protocol and participating veterinary oncologists.

## Why the Caution from Oncologists Is Not Pedantry

A cancer researcher writing in The Conversation in March described the treatment as a one-off, made just for Rosie, and urged readers not to mistake a single animal's response for evidence that the approach works.

The underlying science is not fringe. Personalized neoantigen mRNA vaccines have been in human development for over a decade, and Moderna and Merck's melanoma candidate has produced randomized data. Rosie's case did not invent that field. What it demonstrated, as industry observers noted, is that the design steps have become accessible enough for a determined outsider working with academic collaborators.

Whether the approach helps dogs in general is what the Australian studies are meant to answer, and they have not yet answered it. Pet owners facing a cancer diagnosis should work through a board-certified veterinary oncologist rather than treating a viral case as a treatment plan. Nothing here is approved, and no outcome data across multiple animals have been published.

## Key Questions Answered

What happened to Rosie? Her tumors shrank after the personalized mRNA vaccine, and she entered remission. The company says her cancer returned following a later surgery and writes about her in the past tense.

Did AI create the vaccine? AI tools helped plan the work, filter mutations, and model protein structures, and reporting indicates Grok was used for the final construct. The physical vaccine was made by researchers at UNSW.

Does Rosie's case prove the approach works? No. It is one animal with no control group, alongside surgery, chemotherapy, and immunotherapy. Her tumor grade was never made public, which matters for interpreting the response.

What is Gamgee? The startup Conyngham founded. It launched Aug. 17, 2026, with a $4 million seed round led by Founders Fund, and develops personalized mRNA cancer vaccines for dogs.

This study aimed to estimate the incidence of canine brain tumours in Australia, assess spatio-temporal patterns, explore tumour type-dog breed relationships, evaluate post-diagnosis survival for selected brain tumours, and identify animal-level risk factors. Brain tumours are defined as abnormal cell growth within the cranial cavity^{1}; they are relatively rare but a clinically important cause of neurological disease in dogs^{2}. Brain tumours are classified as primary or secondary. Primary tumours arise from central nervous system tissues such as neurons, glial cells, or meninges, whereas secondary tumours developed through metastatic spread or direct extension from nearby structures, including the pituitary, nasal cavity or skull^{3}.

# Cats could help scientists better understand human cancer, study says

A study of nearly 500 domestic cats uncovered similarities between cancer gene mutations in felines and humans.

May 30, 2026

5 min

Summary loading Loading...

(iStock)

Image

By Kyle Melnick

Louise van der Weyden is a dog person. But as a scientist who studies cancer in animals, she has turned her attention to cats in recent years.

The finding came from a study in which van der Weyden and other scientists across the world investigated cancer-causing genes in tumor samples of nearly 500 domestic cats — specifically which genes were commonly mutated.

The most striking similarity was in a gene called FBXW7, a critical tumor suppressor for people and cats. In cats, the gene was frequently altered in mammary tumors. Mutations in the gene are also associated with worse outcomes for people who have breast cancer.

# Find a clinical trial

Search for a clinical trial in our online registry, or find out about other websites and registries that provide information about clinical trials.

## Search the online registry

Use our search function to start looking for a clinical trial. All clinical trials displayed on this website are sourced from the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry (ANZCTR). The ANZCTR includes all clinical trials with a recruitment site in Australia that are registered on ANZCTR as well as ClinicalTrials.gov, the US clinical trials registry.

  * Basic search
  * Advanced search

## Other registries

There are other clinical trial registries that provide information on trials in Australia, New Zealand and, in some cases, other countries.

Each site will explain how to search the site for trials by the disease or condition that you are interested in. Some websites also allow you to register your details so you can:

  * receive information on potentially suitable trials when they become available
  * allow researchers to access your information and approach you directly.

### Registry list

The International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) aims to provide a single point of access to information about ongoing and completed clinical trials provided by registries around the world. ANZCTR is one of these registries.

The following Australian websites include listings of clinical trials specific to their 
area of expertise:

# Clinical trials

Research is ongoing to find new ways to diagnose and treat a range of cancers. You may be invited to participant in a clinical trial to test new treatments.

A clinical trial is a research study that tests and compares different ways of improving people’s health. Trials may look at whether a treatment is safe, its side effects or how well a treatment or procedure works. Some trials look at how well treatments control symptoms or whether they improve quality of life. 

The main purpose of a clinical trial is to find out whether a new treatment is safe and effective. New medicines are first tested in the laboratory before being tested on people in trials. 

Australian Cancer Trials is a free information service that shows you the latest clinical trials in cancer care, including trials that are currently recruiting participants. # Lumina FAPI PET-CT trial

## Early Breast Cancer clinical trials for Other

Recruiting

Updated: October 14, 2026

### The new clinical trial is recruiting from October 2024 in Auckland, Waikato, Bay of Plenty and Palmerston North. The trial aims to use a newly discovered radioactive tracer called Fibroblast Activation Protein Inhibitor (FAPI) in CT imaging to accurately diagnose and stage lobular breast cancers.
People with lobular breast cancer are encouraged to speak to their medical team about eligibility.

Lobular breast cancer is the second most common type of breast cancer, with around 450 women diagnosed in New Zealand each year. Rather than forming a lump or a mass, lobular breast cancer cells are more unnoticeable as they grow along single layers, making it harder to detect on a mammogram. Complexities in diagnosis and response to treatment mean patients with lobular breast cancer are far likelier to either receive more aggressive treatment than necessary or insufficient treatment, putting them at greater risk of their cancer returning or spreading.

Trial will involve 50 lobular breast cancer patients recruited from around the country who will receive a PET CT scan. The radiotracer FAPI will be used during the scan which binds with cancerous cells to indicate whether the cancer has spread and pinpoint where it has spread to. If there are areas of cancer that haven’t shown up on previous imaging, a radiologist will determine whether the patient was initially incorrectly staged, and the patient’s wider clinical team will assess if a different treatment pathway should be recommended.
